speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Minister for Communications and Information (a) what proportion of Government documents that are more than 25 years old and hence are part of the public archives are contained in the publicly accessible NAS Archives Online; and (b) what proportion of Government documents declassified each year for the past five years have become part of the publicly accessible NAS Archives Online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, when the record is already on NAS, I would like to ask if the Government can consider making it available to everyone on the NAS Online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand right now that there are still some conditions or restrictions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: People have to write in to seek approval.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That approval is sometimes conditionally given on the basis of whether they are using it for research, publishing it or just using it for personal reference.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can documents that have already been declassified – presumably, those sensitivities are not there or there has been redaction – can those be made more freely available to everyone who would like to view it on the NAS Online?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second supplementary question relates to a timeframe.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that after 25 years, these documents are released and they go through a process of review for whether they can be released.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the point of 25 years, there could be certain personal sensitivities, confidentiality obligations, but is there a process to review documents further down the line because those personal sensitivities may not be there, say, 50 years down the line?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there a process to review documents which have been held back from the NAS Online, but perhaps, if there were reviewed again further down the line, they could be released, say, in 50 years' time?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My last supplementary question is on the definition of researcher.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of the access is given on the basis of whether you are doing research, whether you are a researcher.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does one have to be a faculty member in a relevant discipline at a university, or can one be, for example, a private citizen, who has an interest in the matter who wishes to write a book on the matter?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can one be an undergraduate or a graduate student?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the operating definition of "researcher" that is used to give access in cases where access is given only for research purposes?

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: First, if I understand it correctly, the Member is referring to whether more declassified documents can be made viewable to everyone on the online portal.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In fact, on the online portal, if you do a search, you will find that there are quite a number of documents there that are already viewable in full and they can also be seen in portable document format (PDF) form.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Our intention is to make more of these available.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To the Member's question on timeframe, if I understand him correctly, what he means is that: for even older documents, will there be a review process to look at those that have not at first been deemed suitable for public access and then to relook at them again.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I should explain to the Member that our priority is to declassify.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: So, there is quite a lot of work to go through for the current number of records that are 25 years and older.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will take the Member's suggestion into consideration.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: But really, the priority is to declassify as many documents as we can and to encourage our agencies to do so and to help us in doing that.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is also explained in our NLB Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In relation to my first supplementary question, actually my question was on those documents that have been declassified and released already on to the NAS Online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think there are 160,000 of two million.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For those documents that have already been declassified and already on the NAS Online platform, can they be made available more freely?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because, from what I understand, when you go online to this platform, you can view documents and if you click on it, you will not actually get the document.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In some cases, you have to ask for written permission and, in some cases, conditional permission is given.
